entities.name: Anti-Fascist Assembly
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ, Antifašističko Vijeće Narodnog Oslobođenja Jugoslavije), convened first at Bihać in November 1942 and then as the Second Session at Jajce in November 1943 — where it declared itself the supreme legislative and executive body of Yugoslavia — was the wartime parliament through which Josip Broz Tito's Partisans established the legal foundations of socialist Yugoslavia, simultaneously organizing the anti-Nazi resistance and laying the constitutional groundwork for the postwar state.

The Second Session at Jajce (November 29, 1943) was AVNOJ's defining moment: it declared Yugoslavia a federal state of equal peoples, established Tito as Marshal and chairman of the National Committee (effectively Prime Minister), stripped the royal government-in-exile of legitimacy, and banned King Peter II from returning. These decisions — made in a liberated provincial town while the German-Italian occupation still controlled most of Yugoslavia — constituted a revolutionary act of constitutional self-determination within wartime conditions.

AVNOJ's constitutional framework became the basis of socialist Yugoslavia. The multinational federation (six republics and two autonomous provinces) reflected AVNOJ's founding principle of South Slavic 'brotherhood and unity' among Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Bosnians, Macedonians, and Montenegrins. The November 29 date (1943 AVNOJ session) became Yugoslavia's national day. The AVNOJ constitutional model — and its tensions around republic-level national identities — directly foreshadowed the ethnic and constitutional conflicts that led to Yugoslavia's violent dissolution in the 1990s.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: AVNOJ — the wartime parliament that constitutionally founded socialist Yugoslavia in a liberated village while Nazi occupation continued, establishing the six-republic federal framework that both united and ultimately dissolved the South Slavic nations — is one of the most consequential wartime legislative acts in 20th-century European history.
